readingInstruction: Read Psalm 119:41-96. Today’s section moves from steadfast love to affliction. Notice how the psalmist finds comfort in God’s word in suffering.
settingTheScene: This is the second reading from Psalm 119, covering stanzas four through eleven. The psalmist is under pressure. Insolent people mock him, and he suffers affliction. Yet again and again, he turns to the word of God, which he finds to be his comfort, his song, and his life. The section includes some of the most famous lines of the whole psalm.
observation: “Let your steadfast love come to me, O LORD, your salvation according to your promise” (v. 41).
“And I shall walk in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts” (v. 45).
“This is my comfort in my affliction, that your promise gives me life” (v. 50).
“Your statutes have been my songs in the house of my sojourning” (v. 54).
“The LORD is my portion; I promise to keep your words” (v. 57).
“It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes” (v. 71).
“Forever, O LORD, your word is firmly fixed in the heavens” (v. 89).
“If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction” (v. 92).
interpretation:
Verse 41 begins with a request for God’s steadfast love. The psalmist asks that God’s covenant love come to him, according to his promise. The word of God and the love of God are tied together. The promise is the way God’s love reaches us.

The theme of affliction threads through the section. The psalmist does not say that God’s word makes life painless. He says that it is his comfort in affliction. “Your promise gives me life.” The promise is what keeps him alive when everything else is hard. A believer in difficult times needs something to hold, and God’s word is it. The psalmist even makes songs from the statutes “in the house of my sojourning.” He sings the word in a foreign place.

The most challenging line is verse 71: “It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes.” It is a statement made in hindsight. The writer does not say that suffering is pleasant. He says that it taught him. Affliction drove him to God’s word and made him learn what comfort cannot. And verse 67: “Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word.” Trouble corrected him.

The psalm also says the LORD is his portion, as the Levites had no land but God himself as their inheritance. For the psalmist, owning God is greater than owning anything else.

Verse 89 stands as a statement of confidence: “Forever, O LORD, your word is firmly fixed in the heavens.” Human opinions shift. Cultures change. God’s word does not. His faithfulness continues to all generations, and the earth established by him endures. And verse 92 is a stark acknowledgment: “If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished.”
connection: Jesus said, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35). Romans 8:28 says God works all things for good for those who love him, echoing verse 71. Hebrews 12:11 speaks of the peaceful fruit of discipline. 2 Corinthians 1:3-5 describes God as the Father of mercies and God of all comfort. Peter writes that the word of the Lord remains forever (1 Peter 1:25).
application:
If you are in affliction, name one promise from Scripture to hold on to this week.

Look back at a hardship and ask what God taught you through it.

Sing or read aloud a verse of Scripture in a hard place, as the psalmist did.
prayerPrompts: Ask for God’s steadfast love according to his promise.
Tell him where his promise gives you life in affliction.
Ask him to fix his word in your heart.
